uncited: The method constructs an interpolant by analyzing the sequence of Marching Cases encountered as the isovalue sweeps through the data.
For simplicial meshes, distinct vertex isovalues are assumed.
For multi-linear meshes (cubes), the method acknowledges inherent non-linearity.

*   **Output:** A continuous surface representation defined by the union of contour fragments swept out by the Marching Cases, along with associated geometric properties (area, length) as functions of the isovalue.
The core data structure is a **Finite State Machine (FSM)** representing all possible sequences of Marching Cases.
*   **Transitions:** Occur as vertices change from "white" (above isovalue) to "black" (below isovalue) during an isovalue sweep.
**Identify Vertex Order:** Determine the order in which vertices are swept past as the isovalue decreases from high to low.
This order dictates the sequence of cases.
**Construct FSM:** Map all possible sequences of Marching Cases based on the vertex sweep order.
**Define Contour Fragments:** For each case in a path, define the contour fragment using linear interpolation along the cell edges.
**Sweep Surface:** As the isovalue changes, the contour fragment moves.
**Compute Geometric Properties:** Calculate area and length for the swept surfaces.
For simplicial meshes, this involves summing polynomial terms.
For a bilinear cell, the contour is a hyperbola.
*   $x_v$ is the x-coordinate of the vertical asymptote.
*   $y_h$ is the y-coordinate of the horizontal asymptote.
*   **Time Complexity:** Tracking geometric properties via summation of polynomial terms is O(1) size for simplicial meshes.
*   **Memory Complexity:** O(1) for simplicial meshes when summing polynomial terms.
Requires accurate analysis of MC cases to determine integration bounds.
